nameStory: The Can-of-worms Lichen gets its quirky name from the way its tiny, dark fruiting bodies emerge from bark like little worms poking out of holes. When you spot a cluster of these small, cylindrical structures dotting tree bark, it really does look like someone opened a can of fishing bait! The scientific name 'urceolata' means 'pitcher-shaped,' referring to the urn-like form of its reproductive structures.
description: Can-of-worms Lichen is a crustose lichen that forms thin, often barely visible patches on tree bark. Unlike the leafy or branching lichens you might picture, this one creates a subtle crust that's easily overlooked until you notice its distinctive dark, pin-head sized fruiting bodies. These tiny structures, called apothecia, poke up from the bark surface like miniature dark cylinders. The whole organism typically covers just a few square inches of bark surface.

idTips.label: Cylindrical fruiting bodies
idTips.description: Look for tiny dark brown to black cylinders, about 1mm tall, that stick up from bark like little pegs or worms emerging from holes. They feel firm when gently pressed with a fingernail.

idTips.label: Bark-hugging growth
idTips.description: Forms a thin, inconspicuous crust that's often grayish or whitish, blending so well with bark that you might miss it entirely until you spot the dark fruiting structures.

idTips.label: Clustered arrangement
idTips.description: Fruiting bodies typically appear in small groups or scattered clusters, not as single isolated structures, creating that 'handful of worms' appearance.

idTips.label: Smooth bark preference
idTips.description: Most commonly found on relatively smooth-barked trees and shrubs rather than deeply furrowed bark where it would be harder to establish.

habitat: Can-of-worms Lichen grows on the bark of various deciduous trees and shrubs throughout New England's forests. It particularly favors trees with relatively smooth bark like maples, birches, and younger oaks in mixed woodlands. You'll find it from sea level to moderate elevations, often in areas with decent air quality since lichens are sensitive to pollution.

seasonality.spring: Fruiting bodies are visible and well-developed, making this the easiest time to spot this otherwise cryptic lichen. The dark cylinders stand out nicely against fresh bark.
seasonality.summer: Continues to be identifiable by its distinctive fruiting structures, though hot, dry periods may cause the lichen crust to appear more faded or inconspicuous.
seasonality.fall: Still readily identifiable, and the fallen leaves make it easier to spot the dark fruiting bodies against bark. This is another excellent season for lichen hunting.
seasonality.winter: Fruiting bodies remain visible and are often easier to see against snow-dusted bark. The persistent structures make this a reliable year-round identification target.

funFact: Despite being called a lichen, the 'Can-of-worms' is actually not a true lichen at all — it's a fungus that lives on other lichens as a parasite, essentially being a lichen's lichen! This makes it what scientists call a 'lichenicolous fungus' — a fungus that makes its living by parasitizing the algae-fungus partnerships we call lichens.
confusionNotes: The tiny dark fruiting bodies might be confused with small insect eggs or tiny fungi, but unlike eggs, these structures are firmly attached and won't scrape off easily. Unlike most other small bark fungi, these maintain their distinctive cylindrical 'worm-like' shape rather than being round dots or irregular bumps.
contextualKnowledge: The name 'lichen' is somewhat misleading here since this organism is actually a fungal parasite of true lichens rather than a lichen itself. This represents an interesting case where common names don't always reflect the true biological relationships, similar to how killer whales aren't actually whales but are the largest dolphins.
compareHints: Can-of-worms Lichen differs from its relative Stictis radiata by its more cylindrical, worm-like fruiting bodies rather than the flatter, more disc-shaped structures of S. radiata. The 'can-of-worms' appearance is quite distinctive — S. radiata's fruiting bodies look more like tiny dark buttons pressed into the bark rather than little cylinders poking out.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Compared to its relative the Can-of-worms Lichen (Stictis urceolata), Stictis radiata has the distinctive radiating crack pattern rather than the irregularly wavy, worm-like surface texture of its cousin.
